claim: PrePPI contains more than 1.35 million predicted protein-protein interactions (PPIs).
source: We present a database, PrePPI (Predicting Protein-Protein Interactions), of more than 1.35 million predicted protein-protein interactions (PPIs).
evidence: The abstract directly states the size of the PrePPI database.

claim: At least 127,000 PrePPI predictions are expected to constitute direct physical interactions.
source: Of these at least 127,000 are expected to constitute direct physical interactions although the actual number may be much larger (~500,000).
evidence: The abstract provides a specific number based on analysis of the database.

claim: The actual number of direct physical interactions in PrePPI may be as large as 500,000.
source: Of these at least 127,000 are expected to constitute direct physical interactions although the actual number may be much larger (~500,000).
evidence: The abstract provides an estimated range based on analysis.

claim: PrePPI contains predicted interactions for about 85% of the human proteome.
source: The current PrePPI, which contains predicted interactions for about 85% of the human proteome, is related to an earlier version but is based on additional sources of interaction evidence and is far larger in scope.
evidence: The abstract states the coverage of the human proteome.

claim: The use of structural relationships allows PrePPI to infer numerous previously unreported interactions.
source: The use of structural relationships allows PrePPI to infer numerous previously unreported interactions.
evidence: The abstract claims that structural information enables discovery of novel interactions.

claim: PrePPI has been validated by reproducing known interactions.
source: PrePPI has been subjected to a series of validation tests including reproducing known interactions, recapitulating multi-protein complexes, analysis of disease associated SNPs, and identifying functional relationships between interacting proteins.
evidence: The abstract lists validation tests performed on PrePPI.

claim: PrePPI has been validated by recapitulating multi-protein complexes.
source: PrePPI has been subjected to a series of validation tests including reproducing known interactions, recapitulating multi-protein complexes, analysis of disease associated SNPs, and identifying functional relationships between interacting proteins.
evidence: The abstract lists validation tests performed on PrePPI.

claim: PrePPI has been validated by analysis of disease associated SNPs.
source: PrePPI has been subjected to a series of validation tests including reproducing known interactions, recapitulating multi-protein complexes, analysis of disease associated SNPs, and identifying functional relationships between interacting proteins.

claim: Predicted interaction partners can be used to annotate a protein's function using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA).
source: We show, using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), that predicted interaction partners can be used to annotate a protein's function.
evidence: The abstract states a finding from GSEA analysis.

claim: PrePPI provides annotations for most human proteins, including many annotated as having unknown function.
source: We provide annotations for most human proteins, including many annotated as having unknown function.
evidence: The abstract states the scope of functional annotations provided.

claim: PPIs can be classified as direct, indirect, or functional.
source: PPIs can be classified as: (1) direct, when two proteins interact through physical contacts; (2) indirect, when the two proteins bind to the same molecules but are not themselves in physical contact; and (3) functional, when two proteins are functionally related but do not interact directly or indirectly – for example, if they are in the same pathway.
evidence: The introduction provides a classification scheme based on established knowledge.

claim: Direct interactions occur when two proteins interact through physical contacts.
source: PPIs can be classified as: (1) direct, when two proteins interact through physical contacts
evidence: The introduction defines direct interactions based on established knowledge.

claim: Indirect interactions occur when two proteins bind to the same molecules but are not themselves in physical contact.
source: (2) indirect, when the two proteins bind to the same molecules but are not themselves in physical contact
evidence: The introduction defines indirect interactions based on established knowledge.

claim: Functional interactions occur when two proteins are functionally related but do not interact directly or indirectly.
source: (3) functional, when two proteins are functionally related but do not interact directly or indirectly – for example, if they are in the same pathway.
evidence: The introduction defines functional interactions based on established knowledge.

claim: Achieving complete coverage of PPIs remains difficult.
source: Considerable experimental effort has been devoted to identifying and cataloging PPIs, but achieving complete coverage remains difficult (Hart et al., 2006).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this claim about the state of the field.

claim: PPIs identified by high-throughput methods are dominated by interactions supported by only one experiment.
source: The PPIs identified by these methods have been deposited in a range of databases (Ruepp et al., 2010; Stark et al., 2011; Licata et al., 2012) but are dominated by interactions supported by only one experiment, and can be of uncertain reliability (Sprinzak et al., 2003; Venkatesan et al., 2009; Rolland et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites references to support this claim about the quality of experimental data.

claim: PPIs identified by high-throughput methods can be of uncertain reliability.
source: The PPIs identified by these methods have been deposited in a range of databases (Ruepp et al., 2010; Stark et al., 2011; Licata et al., 2012) but are dominated by interactions supported by only one experiment, and can be of uncertain reliability (Sprinzak et al., 2003; Venkatesan et al., 2009; Rolland et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites references to support this claim about data reliability.

claim: Recent state-of-the-art applications of two-hybrid and MS-based approaches provide interactions for only one-quarter to one-third of the human proteome.
source: Moreover, even recent state-of-the-art applications of two-hybrid (Rolland et al., 2014) and MS-based approaches (Havugimana et al., 2012; Hein et al., 2015; Huttlin et al., 2015; Wan et al., 2015), using protocols involving multiple experiments to ensure quality control, provide interactions for only one-quarter to one-third of the human proteome.
evidence: The introduction cites references to support this claim about coverage limitations.

claim: Automatic literature curation has produced large databases such as STRING.
source: Automatic literature curation has produced large databases such as STRING (Franceschini et al., 2013), but necessarily these are primarily comprised of proteins whose biological importance is already known (Rolland et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites references to support this claim about computational approaches.

claim: Literature-curated databases are primarily comprised of proteins whose biological importance is already known.
source: Automatic literature curation has produced large databases such as STRING (Franceschini et al., 2013), but necessarily these are primarily comprised of proteins whose biological importance is already known (Rolland et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this claim about bias in curated databases.

claim: Curated interactions are often leveraged to predict additional PPIs using evidence such as sequence similarity.
source: However, curated interactions are often leveraged to predict additional PPIs using evidence such as sequence similarity (Walhout et al., 2000; Sprinzak and Margalit, 2001), evolutionary history (Lichtarge and sowa, 2002; Lewis et al., 2010; de Juan et al., 2013), expression profiles (Jansen et al., 2002; Bhardwaj and Lu, 2005), and genomic location (Marcotte et al., 1999).
evidence: The introduction cites references to support this claim about computational prediction methods.

claim: HumanNet contains 450,000 PPIs for about 15,500 human proteins of which about 400,000 correspond to computational predictions.
source: For example, HumanNet (Lee et al., 2011) contains 450,000 PPIs for about 15,500 human proteins of which about 400,000 correspond to computational predictions.
evidence: The introduction cites a reference and provides specific numbers about HumanNet.

claim: STRING contains 311,000 interactions based primarily on literature curation for about 15,000 human proteins.
source: STRING (Franceschini et al., 2013) contains 311,000 interactions based primarily on literature curation for about 15,000 human proteins.
evidence: The introduction cites a reference and provides specific numbers about STRING.

claim: Large computational databases contain evidence for all three categories of PPIs (direct, indirect, and functional).
source: These large computational databases contain evidence for all three categories of PPIs.
evidence: The introduction makes an inference about the content of computational databases.

claim: Large computational databases do not exploit structural information.
source: On the other hand, they do not exploit structural information which is perhaps the strongest evidence for a direct physical interaction.
evidence: The introduction makes a claim about limitations of other computational databases.

claim: Structural information is perhaps the strongest evidence for a direct physical interaction.
source: On the other hand, they do not exploit structural information which is perhaps the strongest evidence for a direct physical interaction.
evidence: The introduction makes a claim about the value of structural information based on scientific reasoning.

claim: PrePPI combines structural information with different sources of non-structural information.
source: We recently developed a PPI prediction method (Zhang et al., 2012), PrePPI, which combines structural information with different sources of non-structural information.
evidence: The introduction cites the previous PrePPI paper to describe the method.

claim: PrePPI is a low-resolution method that enabled the use of protein structural information on a genome-wide scale.
source: In contrast to structure-based approaches that depend on detailed modeling or binding mode sampling (Lu et al., 2002; Tuncbag et al., 2011; Mosca et al., 2013), we developed a low-resolution method that enabled the use of protein structural information on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: The introduction cites references and describes the PrePPI approach.

claim: The previous version of PrePPI provides about 300,000 'reliable' interactions for ~13,300 proteins.
source: Applied to the human proteome, the resulting database (Zhang et al., 2012) performs comparably to HT approaches and provides about 300,000 'reliable' interactions for ~13,300 proteins (see below).
evidence: The introduction cites the previous PrePPI paper and provides specific numbers.

claim: PrePPI relies heavily on the 'structural Blast' approach.
source: PrePPI relies heavily on the 'structural Blast' approach (Dey et al., 2013), where structural alignments between proteins can detect functional relationships that are undetectable with sequence information alone.
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to describe a key component of PrePPI.

claim: Structural alignments between proteins can detect functional relationships that are undetectable with sequence information alone.
source: PrePPI relies heavily on the 'structural Blast' approach (Dey et al., 2013), where structural alignments between proteins can detect functional relationships that are undetectable with sequence information alone.
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this claim about structural alignments.

claim: The use of structural information in PrePPI is largely responsible for the prediction of a large number of PPIs not inferred with other approaches.
source: The use of structural information in PrePPI is largely responsible for the prediction of a large number of PPIs not inferred with other approaches.
evidence: The introduction makes a claim about the unique contribution of structural information.

claim: The updated version of PrePPI incorporates additional interaction evidence based on methodological advances in the use of structure, orthology, RNA expression profiles, and predicted interactions between structured domains and peptides.
source: As illustrated in Figure 1, the evidence is based on methodological advances in the use of structure, orthology, RNA expression profiles, and predicted interactions between structured domains and peptides (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction references Figure 1 and cites a paper to describe new evidence types.

claim: The resulting PrePPI database contains over 1.35 million reliably predicted interactions with considerably increased accuracy compared to the previous version.
source: The resulting PrePPI database contains over 1.35 million reliably predicted interactions with considerably increased accuracy compared to the previous version.
evidence: The introduction states the size and improved accuracy of the new database.

claim: Reliable predictions are made for ~17,200 human proteins in the updated PrePPI.
source: Moreover, reliable predictions are made for ~17,200 human proteins, about 85% of the human proteome.
evidence: The introduction provides specific numbers about protein coverage.

claim: By combining PrePPI and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), essentially all of the human proteome can be annotated based on the known functions of their predicted interactors.
source: Further, by combining PrePPI and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), essentially all of the human proteome—including 2000 proteins of unknown function—can be annotated based on the known functions of their predicted interactors.
evidence: The introduction states a finding about functional annotation capability.

claim: PrePPI can annotate 2000 proteins of unknown function using GSEA.
source: Further, by combining PrePPI and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), essentially all of the human proteome—including 2000 proteins of unknown function—can be annotated based on the known functions of their predicted interactors.
evidence: The introduction provides a specific number of proteins of unknown function that can be annotated.

claim: The Bayesian network was trained on a positive reference set of 42,636 yeast PPIs compiled from various PPI databases and reported in at least two publications.
source: The Bayesian network was trained on a positive reference set of 42,636 yeast PPIs compiled from various PPI databases and reported in at least two publications (the yeast HC reference set) and a negative set of all pairs for which there is no literature evidence of an interaction (the yeast N set).
evidence: The Results section describes the training procedure with specific numbers.

claim: The Bayesian network was evaluated with a positive reference set of 26,983 human interactions reported in at least two publications.
source: The Bayesian network was evaluated with a positive reference set of 26,983 human interactions reported in at least two publications (the human HC reference set) and a negative reference set consisting of 1,632,716 pairs of proteins where each individual protein belongs to a separate cellular compartment as annotated by GO (the human N set; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The Results section describes the evaluation procedure with specific numbers.

claim: The addition of new evidence considerably increases the true positive rate at low false positive rates.
source: The addition of new evidence considerably increases the true positive rate at low false positive rates (solid black and gray curves).
evidence: The Results section references Figure 2a to support this claim about performance improvement.

claim: At a similar false positive rate, PrePPI performance is comparable to that of Y2H and BioPlex databases.
source: As can be seen, at a similar false positive rate (FPR), PrePPI performance is comparable to that of these two databases.
evidence: The Results section references Figure 2a to support this comparison.

claim: PrePPI recovers essentially no RRS interactions for LR>600.
source: The fact that PrePPI recovers essentially no RRS interactions for LR>600 provides an independent validation of this definition of a reliable prediction.
evidence: The Results section references Figure 2b to support this validation claim.

claim: About 60% of the PRS database is recovered at LR cutoff of 600.
source: About 60% of the PRS database is recovered at this LR cutoff while approximately 50% of the human HC reference set is also recovered.

claim: The Y2H database recovers ~7% of the PRS interactions.
source: Figure 2b also shows that the Y2H and Bioplex databases recover ~7% and ~16% of the PRS interactions, respectively.

source: Figure 2b also shows that the Y2H and Bioplex databases recover ~7% and ~16% of the PRS interactions, respectively.

source: The current PrePPI database contains about 1.35 million reliable PPI predictions, a significant increase over the 300,000 PPIs in the previous version.

evidence: The Results section provides specific numbers about the contribution of new structural data.

claim: The use of homology models leads to a clear improvement in PrePPI performance.

claim: The odds ratio for disease-associated SNPs to be in PrePPI predicted interfaces is statistically significant with a Z-score of ~41.
source: The Z-score for the enrichment of disease associated SNPs in interfaces was ~41 and for the depletion of benign SNPs was ~35, implying the odds ratios we find are statistically significant.
evidence: The Materials and methods section references Table 5 and provides specific Z-scores.
